name: Stackby
subcategory: spreadsheet databases and operational data apps
tagline: Build a small table-based operational tracker with views and API columns

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: 5 editors plus 50 read-only guests; 20 stacks; 1,500 rows/stack; 2 GB attachments/stack; 100 internal automations; 2 MB uploads; 1 app/stack; 2-week history; 2 linked API columns.

tiers.name: Economy
tiers.limits: 25 stacks; 7,000 rows/stack; 6 GB attachments/stack; 1,000 internal automations; 500 automatic API runs; 5 MB uploads; 3 apps/stack; 6-month history.
tiers.notes: Annual rate is displayed per user, but annual checkout starts at 3 users ($149/year total).

tiers.name: Business
tiers.limits: 50 stacks; 50,000 rows/stack; 20 GB attachments/stack; 25,000 internal automations; 1,000 automatic API runs; 25 MB uploads; 10 apps/stack; 1-year history.
tiers.notes: Annual checkout starts at 3 users ($299/year total).

tiers.name: Pro
tiers.limits: 100 stacks; 100,000 rows/stack; 50 GB attachments/stack; 100,000 internal automations; 5,000 automatic API runs; 50 MB uploads; 20 apps/stack; 1-year history.
tiers.notes: Annual checkout starts at 3 users ($449/year total). The comparison table also labels this tier 'Business Plus.'

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Unlimited stacks; 250,000 rows/stack; 250,000 internal automations; 10,000 automatic API runs; 3-year history.
tiers.notes: Quote required. The live card says 1,000 GB attachment storage while the live comparison table says 100 GB.

pricing.freeTierCaps: 5 editors, 50 read-only guests, 20 stacks, 1,500 rows/stack, 2 GB attachments/stack, 100 internal automations, 2 MB uploads, 1 app/stack, 2-week history and 2 linked API columns
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual; annual plans are sold in fixed team-size increments beginning at 3 users and advertise savings up to 70%
pricing.hiddenCosts: Annual checkout requires 3, 6, 10, 15 or larger preset seat quantities; paid editor/creator seats added mid-cycle are prorated; portal add-ons start at $60, $100 or $150 per 10 portal guests/month depending on plan; exceeding automation/API limits stops further runs.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For Stackby, build a small table-based operational tracker with views and API columns. The hard boundary is templates, integrations, api columns, collaboration, and hosted sync, plus data model flexibility, collaboration, and integrations.
coreLoopDIY: Build a small table-based operational tracker with structured records, provide grid, form, kanban, and filtered views, and expose a documented API.
whatYouLose: templates, integrations, API columns, collaboration, and hosted sync
moatNotes: data model flexibility, collaboration, and integrations
ongoingBurden: schema changes, formulas, permissions, imports, attachments, views, APIs, concurrency, backups, and migrations
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Stackby because teams pay when a flexible database becomes a shared operational system with integrations and years of accumulated business logic. The recurring cost buys schema changes, formulas, permissions, imports, attachments, views, APIs, concurrency, backups, and migrations, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: NocoDB
priorArt.desc: Active open-source no-code database interface and Airtable alternative.

alternatives.name: Stackby Free
alternatives.desc: The same product's free plan does the actual job: 20 stacks, 1,500 rows each, two API columns, views, and 100 automations.

rejectedAlternatives.name: NocoDB Free
rejectedAlternatives.desc: A good table workspace, but it has no linked API-column feature, the reason to use Stackby in the first place.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Rows Free
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The famous connected-spreadsheet alternative is being folded into Superhuman Docs, so it is not a durable new home.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Personal plan and a small-team structured database DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Stackby in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, and Docker Compose; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: build a small table-based operational tracker with structured records, provide grid, form, kanban, and filtered views, and expose a documented API.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create workspaces, bases, tables, fields, records, attachments, relations, and saved views.
Support text, number, currency, date, boolean, select, formula-lite, and relation field types.
Build grid, form, kanban, and record-detail views from one canonical schema.
Add role-based permissions, optimistic concurrency checks, audit history, and trash restore.
Provide CSV import or export and a token-authenticated REST API generated from the schema.
Ship migrations, seed data, backups, health checks, and a schema export format.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out full spreadsheet formula compatibility.
Deliberately leave out hundreds of automations and integrations.
Deliberately leave out large-enterprise governance and vendor-managed scale.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
